At the level of illustrative application, the work takes as its privileged <1>locus</1> the ecosystem of products and services of the multinational <2>Riot Games</2>, with a focus on the game <3>p. 37</3> <4>League of </4> <5>Legends</5> and its extensions on associated platforms. This scope does not seek to exhaust the diversity of the global interactive entertainment industry, but to offer a field of exemplification in which typical structures of semiotic governance, practices of hypercuratorial anticipation, monetization models based on digital goods and recurring patterns of friction between consumers and supplier become particularly clear. Although the IOC is built to engage with continuous digital consumption as a whole, the research limits its use of references to this universe to supporting intelligibility and anchoring the theoretical-dogmatic path.

Through the grammar of tolls, monetization strategies cease to be mere marketing accessories and come to compose the very functional substance of the <1>p. 201</1> Immaterial Object of Consumption (IOC). The platform institutes a field of choices and expectations mediated by signs, in which micro-drainage and algorithmic opacity deepen the consumer's factual vulnerability in its semiotic feature. As Dowbor suggests, the everyday governance of continuous services recalculates, in real time, parameters of cost, eligibility and access, causing the “product” to be lived as a regime of variable permissions, and not as a thing delivered once and for all. It is in this sense that the mismatch of a dogmatics forged for stable material goods becomes evident when it is confronted with objects whose enjoyment depends on incessant modulations inscribed in the very technical and semiotic architecture of consumption.

The expression <1>Lex Plataformae</1> therefore intends to name not a set of pre-drafted clauses, but a private ordering that is technically executable, economically oriented and semiotically naturalized. Its specificity lies in the fact that the platform not only enunciates rules, but materially conditions the field of the possible. It not only promises sanctions, but implements them. It not only interprets behaviors, but classifies, records, prioritizes, makes invisible, recommends, blocks, expels, restricts, monetizes and reconfigures the very environment in which the user tries to exercise the enjoyment of the acquired object. For this reason, the analogy with the <2>Lex Mercatoria</2> is useful as a point of departure, but insufficient as a point of arrival. The <3>Lex </3> <4>Mercatoria</4> refers, in its best-known formulation, to a transnational order associated with mercantile practices and private mechanisms for stabilizing expectations. <5>p. 28</5> The <6>Lex </6> <7>Plataformae</7>, in turn, designates a private order whose center is not only mercantile circulation among actors, but control of the infrastructure of access, of the intelligibility of the experience and of the concrete conditions for exercising the user's position.

Varoufakis places this new cold war<1><2>183</2></1> at the heart of technofeudalism by arguing that the consolidation of cloud capital reorders interstate competition in terms of infrastructural hegemony. The axis of conflict<3><4>184</4></3> shifts to the command of digital ecosystems, payment regimes and currencies compatible with technofeudal extraction. The tendency, for the author, is the bifurcation of the world system into antagonistic digital superfiefs, with events such as the freezing of Russian reserves working as signals of inflection on the political risk of depending on monetary channels controlled by another power<5><6>185</6></5> <7>Varoufakis</7><8>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 136-141)</8>. At the same time, the intensification of alternatives, such as digital currencies, figures as a strategy for circumventing international transfer channels controlled by the hegemonic power<9><10>186</10></9><11>. </11>Finally, the author suggests global distributive effects, with Europe and the <12>p. 181</12> Global South pressed to choose between territories, standards and currencies, at the cost of lost autonomy and greater vulnerability<13><14>187</14></13>.

The epigraph <1>opens the section</1>, sets its atmosphere and circumscribes the environment of experience in which the legal problem will be confronted. The analytical work of the section comes afterwards. The argument is not founded on the excerpt, nor does it draw its chain of validation from it. What is preserved, through its presence, is the perception that the phenomenon investigated does not fit entirely into the technical-normative language with which Law usually describes it. In a thesis that deals with platforms as structures for conducting behavior, retaining bonds and administering meanings, ignoring the aesthetic thickness of the object in the name of a supposed rigor would only impoverish it.

Tercio Sampaio Ferraz Jr. completes the argument through the function of legal dogmatics. He presents it as a technology geared to action, which carves out what can be handled in the form of a decision, and recalls that the actual legal decision works with incomplete information and that its immediate purpose is to absorb insecurity, turning undecidable incompatibilities into decidable alternatives. On the platform, opacity tends to make the dispute endless, because there is always some technical backstage that could explain the effect. A minimum threshold works as a mechanism of finitude, since it organizes the debate around elements that can be argued in adversarial proceedings.

The methodological basis comes from Miguel Reale and Tercio Sampaio Ferraz Jr. Reale describes the norm as an integration of facts and values, and it is this integration that allows governed enjoyment to be treated as a legally modelable experience. Reale also observes that an unforeseen technical circumstance may alter the meaning and content of a legal text. Ferraz Jr. supplies the safeguard, because dogmatic delimitation works by cutting into reality to isolate the problems relevant to the decision, and dogmatics can deal with this kind of loss only if it is able to make it decidable without falling into descriptive paralysis.

There are two movements. The first is descriptive and recognizes the law of the platform, a technically executable private ordering that functions as the effective floor of conduct before enacted law manages to name it, and which has its own chapter ahead. The second is dogmatic and is not automatic, because the mere fact that this regime governs is not abusive teleology, and the category only makes sense as a controllable attribution, which reconstructs a pattern instead of reacting to an episode. The requirement is consistent with Miguel Reale, for whom law only reaches reality when it converts facts and values into criteria, and with Tercio Sampaio Ferraz Jr., for whom, without categories of structure and recurrence, the decision fragments into microevents.

Moving from diagnosis to the dogmatic category calls for methodological restraint, which three authors provide. Miguel Reale allows patterns to be read as legal facts, because the norm integrates facts and values and the formation of law presupposes the observation of regularities, though this does not license voluntarism. Tercio Sampaio Ferraz Jr. points out that dogmatics cuts out a piece of reality to make conflicts decidable, so the category works as a cutting device that turns diffuse suspicions into verifiable hypotheses, without requiring full transparency of the ecosystem or impossible proof from the consumer. Umberto Eco dispels the confusion between sign and private feeling, and so symbolic promises built into the bundle can be reconstructed as objective components of utility and legitimate expectation.

The lawyer does not need to prove how the algorithm decides. Criteria that required full access to logs and internal rules would make the category unworkable, and Tercio Sampaio Ferraz Jr. reminds us that legal decision operates under uncertainty and does not presuppose complete information. What must be shown is governance relevant to the acquired utility, stable enough to produce patterns of enjoyment and of degradation. The interpreter, in turn, must state which elements of the regime were used, how they connect to the result, and why ordinary variation was distinguished from significant degradation.

The expression digital vulnerability has descriptive usefulness, but little dogmatic yield, because it names the environment in which the injury occurs and does not isolate the mechanism of the asymmetry. The digital works as a marker of setting, and not as an operator of attribution. Tercio Sampaio Ferraz Jr. describes dogmatics as a cut in reality that isolates the problems relevant to the decision, and Miguel Reale holds that there is no raw legal fact. A concept must say what must be proven, which duty was strained and which consequence is appropriate.
